entries.criterion: When I build a world, the build record shows that world's own bookkeeping laws in plain words.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: the AI that designs the world declares its laws (design part 1, approved "yes lets make it companhy plannign complaint")
demonstration: Paste the pencil description and press Create simulation.
When the build finishes, open the build record and read the Laws list.
entries.expected: A short list of sentences in the pencil world's own words, such as "Pencils are made only by assembling them and used up only by a customer" and "A sale moves pencils to the buyer and cash to the seller", each naming things and moves that appear elsewhere on the page.
entries.failure_example: Broken: the Laws list is missing, or a law names something the pencil world does not have (gold, a bank), or the same laws appear word for word for a kitchen description. Working: every law names this world's goods, money and moves.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: a laws table in the build record, each row opening the moves it names

entries.criterion: The engine itself keeps each world's declared laws: a move, or a knock-on effect it sets off, that breaks one is refused, and the page says which law it broke.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: the engine enforces declared laws generically and names the law it refuses on (design part 2)
demonstration: Open the World Builder's replay of the saved pencil13 world, re-built in S2 so that the world design AI wrote its laws (the S2 report gives the link and shows the laws came from the model reply, not a person).
Go to round 8 and find the shop's buy-boxed-pencils move; read what the page says about it.
Open the S2 report's second replay, a world whose move sets off a knock-on effect that breaks a law (for example a fall that would destroy cash), and read that round.
entries.expected: The purchase is marked refused (orange, with the word "refused") beside a law in plain words saying a purchase must move payment the other way; the shop's boxes and the factory's cash are unchanged that round. In the knock-on replay the move that set off the effect is refused the same way, the page names the knock-on effect that broke the law, and nothing from that moment is kept.
entries.failure_example: Broken: the purchase shows as done, boxes move to the shop and no cash moves to the factory (what pencil13 does today); or it is refused with no law named; or the knock-on effect goes through and only the move is undone. Working: refused, law shown, nothing from the moment kept.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: the run's round list with the refusal row opening its law

entries.criterion: An independent review points out where the rules do not match my description, in my description's words.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: an independent AI review of the rules replaces the heuristic checks (design part 3)
demonstration: Open the build record of the saved pencil13 world reviewed in S3 (link given in the S3 report).
entries.expected: Each finding names one rule and quotes the words of the description it was checked against; one finding says buy-boxed-pencils takes the boxes but pays the factory nothing.
entries.failure_example: Broken: the list is empty, says only "looks good", or gives findings without quoting the description. Working: buy-boxed-pencils is named with the quoted description words about the shop buying from the factory.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: a findings table, each row opening its rule and the quoted words

entries.criterion: The pencil world I build runs with every sale paying for what it takes.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-27 "do that": a live pencil build to confirm money changes hands on a sale
demonstration: Open the World Builder, paste the pencil description and press Create simulation.
Let the run play, then open any sale in the round list or the network view.
entries.expected: Each sale moves pencils to the buyer and cash to the seller in the same step, including the shop buying boxes from the factory; the build record lists the laws and the review findings.
entries.failure_example: Broken: a purchase where goods move and cash does not (pencil13's buy-boxed-pencils), or the build fails before the run (pencil14, 422). Working: both sides move on every sale.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: the run's round list and network view

entries.criterion: Moves are still written freely in each world's own terms; there is no fixed menu of move types.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: fixed move types (transfer / exchange / transform) "destorys the whol e potin of what we are doing"
demonstration: Open the World Builder and build the pencil world; open its list of moves.
Build a kitchen description the same way and open its list of moves.
entries.expected: Each world's moves carry its own names and effects (cut cedar, assemble pencils, sell a box; chop, plate, serve), and neither list shows built-in kinds such as transfer, exchange or transform.
entries.failure_example: Broken: every move is labelled with one of a few fixed kinds, or a move the description asks for (a cook tasting a sauce) cannot be written because no kind fits. Working: moves differ per world and the laws sit beside them.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: the moves list in the build record, each move opening its effects and the laws that touch it

entries.criterion: Descriptions the World Builder has never seen, of very different shapes and lengths, each build a world that keeps its own laws, with no code written for any of them.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: the root problems are in the substrate and the world generating and validating process, not one pencil world
Plan S5: four varied descriptions built live in parallel
demonstration: Open the World Builder and build each of four different descriptions in turn: the pencil supply chain, the airfield, a kitchen, and the long Waltzman scenario (people and organizations, not goods).
For each, open the build record's Laws and Review findings, then the run.
Open any refused step, and any sale or hand-over in the run.
entries.expected: Each of the four worlds has laws naming its own things and moves (the Waltzman world may declare few or none, and says so); every refused step names the law it broke, including knock-on effects; every hand-over that a law pairs moves both sides; the review's findings quote that description's own words; all four builds finish.
entries.failure_example: Broken: the laws are the pencil world's laws reworded, a step commits that breaks a listed law (goods appear with no listed move making them), or the build only works for pencils. Working: each description gets its own laws and the run keeps them.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: build record (laws, findings) linked to the run's round list

entries.criterion: Mistakes in a world's rules are caught at the root, by the engine's laws and the independent review, not by a growing list of hand-written checks, one per mistake.
grounded_in: Brian 2026-10-28: "you hjave been fixing symptoms not root problems"
demonstration: Open a finished build record on the World Builder and read the panel that says what checked the rules.
Open the S4 table on this plan's review page: each retired hand-written check, the incident it was added for, and what catches that incident now.
entries.expected: The build record lists three kinds of checking only: the world's declared laws, the review's findings, and reports of what the test run saw. Each retired check in the S4 table points at a saved world where a law refusal or a review finding now catches its incident, and no new hand-written check was added for a new mistake.
entries.failure_example: Broken: the build record still lists checks such as 'goods from nothing' or 'starved holders' guessing at meaning, or a new mistake found in S5 was fixed by adding another such check. Working: the new mistake is traced to a missing law or a review finding and fixed there.

representation.view: composite-linked-view: its table pane lists retired check, incident, saved world and what catches it now

mappings.coverage_reason: A7 requires the S4 table to show every retired hand-written check now caught by a law refusal or review finding, and explicitly checks that no new hand-written check was added; the demonstration fails if mistakes are still caught symptom-by-symptom.
mappings.outcome_reason: Constraints need not appear in the outcome line; the outcome restates the spirit as 'fixed rather than one symptom at a time.'

mappings.coverage_reason: A2 requires the engine to refuse a law-breaking move and name the broken law, which fails directly if the substrate does not enforce declared laws; A6 extends this across four diverse worlds.
mappings.missing: No criterion tests substrate behaviour beyond law enforcement — state persistence, event ordering, world representation, or other capabilities that may also be root problems are unchecked.
mappings.outcome_reason: The outcome says 'the root problems in the substrate…are fixed,' keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A1 requires laws in the world's own words in the build record; A2's demonstration records that those laws came from the model reply; A6 checks generation across four diverse descriptions; all three fail if the world-generating process does not produce law declarations.
mappings.missing: No criterion checks the prompt sent to the model or the internal steps of the generating process; only the output (laws present, attributed to the model) is verified.
mappings.outcome_reason: The outcome says 'whose own bookkeeping laws the AI declares,' keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A3 requires each review finding to name a rule and quote the description, failing if the validating process does not read rules against the description; A6 checks that review findings quote description words across four worlds; A7 requires old hand-written symptom-checks to be retired and replaced by law refusals or review findings.
mappings.missing: No criterion checks whether the review process consults the description text directly or uses another internal mechanism; only the review output is inspected.
mappings.outcome_reason: The outcome says 'whose rules an independent review reads against the description,' keeping this requirement.

mappings.coverage_reason: A5 opens two worlds' move lists and explicitly expects that neither shows built-in kinds such as transfer, exchange or transform; it fails directly if any built-in move types appear.
mappings.outcome_reason: Constraints need not appear in the outcome line; the outcome says 'moves the AI still writes freely,' keeping this constraint.

mappings.coverage_reason: A2's demonstration requires the S2 report to show that the laws came from the model reply, not a person, which fails if the LLM is not the source of world-specific knowledge; no criterion verifies that the LLM uses its domain knowledge to write semantically correct laws.
mappings.missing: No criterion checks that the LLM correctly applies its domain knowledge (e.g., a model that declares trivially wrong or domain-blind laws would pass A2's attribution check but break Brian's requirement that the LLM 'surely does' know what money is).
mappings.outcome_reason: Constraints need not appear in the outcome line; the outcome says 'bookkeeping laws the AI declares,' keeping this constraint.

mappings.coverage_reason: All criteria demonstrate the working world-builder system; none would fail if the planning document used a different format than company planning requires.
mappings.outcome_reason: Process requirements need not appear in the outcome line; the outcome describes the delivered system, not the planning document's format.
